content: In the study by Millard, Bailey, and Hanson (1991), the selection process for attending a maternity waiting home (MWH) was open to all women, with no restrictions. Women considered high-risk and living far from the facility were actively encouraged to stay at the MWH during the last two weeks of pregnancy. In contrast, the study by Gaym, Pearson, and Soe (2012) did not describe the selection process. Chandramohan, Cutts, and Chandra (1994) attempted to control for confounding variables during the analysis stage, despite the lack of randomization between the two groups, which could result in imbalances in known and unknown variables. Two studies (Chandramohan, Cutts, and Chandra, 1994; Gaym, Pearson, and Soe, 2012) did not specify eligibility criteria, while Millard, Bailey, and Hanson (1991) allowed all women to participate. All studies were conducted in sub-Saharan Africa, with most (except Gaym, Pearson, and Soe, 2012) specifying that the settings were rural or remote. The components of the MWHs varied significantly across and within studies, including differences in size, location, facilities, length of stay before delivery, food provision, and additional services such as antenatal care (ANC), health education, and reduced fees for instrumental deliveries or cesarean sections. All studies compared MWHs to standard care prior to facility admission. Consistently, the studies reported a reduction in stillbirth rates following the intervention, and lower perinatal mortality rates were observed among women who used MWHs. The studies were observational and of weak methodological quality, with a high risk of bias due to unclear methods. Data collection methods were deemed reliable in two studies (Chandramohan, Cutts, and Chandra, 1994; Larsen and Muller, 1978), which used hospital records, but no information on validity was provided. In two other studies (Millard, Bailey, and Hanson, 1991; Tumwine and Dungare, 1996), the methods were not described. Recruitment and selection processes were not fully detailed in all studies. For example, Tumwine and Dungare (1996) reported that health center staff or trained traditional birth attendants (TBAs) encouraged women to attend MWHs, while Chandramohan, Cutts, and Chandra (1994) recruited high-risk women. Millard, Bailey, and Hanson (1991) allowed any woman to attend, and Larsen and Muller (1978) provided no details. Blinding of outcome assessors and participants was unclear in all studies. In Chandramohan, Cutts, and Chandra (1994), efforts were made to control for confounders during analysis, despite the lack of randomization. Two studies (Chandramohan, Cutts, and Chandra, 1994; Tumwine and Dungare, 1996) included only high-risk women, although the definition of risk varied. In Millard, Bailey, and Hanson (1991), eligibility was open to all women, with high-risk women encouraged to stay at the MWH. All studies were conducted in sub-Saharan Africa, with settings described as remote. The components of MWHs varied widely, including size, location, facilities, length of stay, food provision, and additional services such as ANC, health education, and reduced fees for instrumental deliveries or cesarean sections. All studies compared MWHs to standard care prior to facility admission. Lower neonatal mortality rates were consistently reported among women admitted to hospitals via MWHs. Regarding community-organized transport schemes, one cluster randomized trial of moderate quality found that women exposed to a multifaceted intervention, which included a small community-organized emergency transport component, were more likely to deliver in a facility. However, the improvements could not be attributed to any single component of the intervention, as lady health workers (LHWs) played a significant role in implementation. Two case-control studies of weak methodological quality reported inconsistent findings, with one study showing an increase in facility births and the other associating community transport plans with a decrease in home births. The overall quality of evidence for these interventions was very low. For partnerships with traditional birth attendants (TBAs), six observational studies (two of moderate and four of weak quality) reported on skilled birth attendance (SBA) or facility births. The interventions varied and were complex, making it difficult to isolate the effects of individual components. Most studies showed an increase in SBA use over time, but the lack of control groups limited the ability to draw firm conclusions. The overall quality of evidence was very low. In terms of culturally appropriate skilled maternity care, two observational studies of weak quality reported on facility births and SBA use. Both studies showed trends toward increased facility births, but the lack of control groups and differences in interventions limited the ability to attribute outcomes to the interventions. The overall quality of evidence was very low.
